strengths: The study addresses an important question on diversity and degeneracy in RNNs.

The authors investigate this question across multiple levels: behavior, dynamics, and connectivity, and across multiple settings: different loss functions, network sizes, and weight regularization methods.
The paper is clearly structured and easy to follow.
The authors tried their method in various tasks and settings.
The authors goal of measuring and controlling the degeneracy across different scales is very important and I think an important question.
The figures are very explanatory and the paper is written well, easy to follow.

The proposed method provides a unified approach to understanding the wide range of solutions in task-trained RNNs. The authors present multiple reasons/possibilities for these solutions (i.e due to behavioral, weight space or neural dynamic variability), and quantify its relationship with the amount of information present in each task.
The information theoretic approach provides a way to categorize more complex v/s less complex tasks, which is then used to observe trends with other covariates.
The authors further increase same task complexity by increasing the amount of information associated with the task (by adding independent channels).
Their results suggest a similar trend in complexity with weight space degeneracy, and an inverse trend for neural dynamics and generalization.
Lastly, they use these insights to increase/decrease the solution-space associated with tasks.
The paper is structured and clear.
Jointly considering several degeneracy metrics (in particular DSA) and tasks is useful for the community.
The tasks considered are diverse and rooted in the literature, giving a considerable degree of generality to the results.
The related works section is thorough and bridges to the feedforward literature
This paper proposes a unified approach to analyze the degeneracy of solutions obtained by RNNs on several tasks from several perspectives.

This paper incorporates certain measures from information theory to quantify task complexity. The authors conclude that an increase in task complexity will lead to a reduction in degeneracy in neural dynamics and generalization behavior. However, it will simultaneously increase the degeneracy in weight space.
Based on their analysis, the authors propose several strategies for controlling solution degeneracy in practical applications.
weaknesses: The central claim of the paper is overly simplistic and may significantly depend on factors that were not considered in the proposed work.

The authors provide little information on how the RNN weights were initialized and there is no analysis on how the main claims may depend on their initial distribution; the decrease in dynamics degeneracy with task complexity may not hold for RNNs initialized with small weights close to zero.

The authors measured weights degeneracy with a stricter Frobenius norm than the dynamical degeneracy; the norm used for DSA is invariant under orthogonal transformation, which is less strict than the permutation invariant norm used to quantify the weights degeneracy, raising questions about how much the result depends on the specific norm and its invariance class.

Task complexity is quantified as the entropy of the task inputs and outputs, which captures only a specific aspect of task complexity; it is invariant under shuffling of timesteps, and it is unclear whether the relationship between degeneracy and task complexity still holds for time‑shuffled variants of the tasks.

The entropy‑based method (measuring input and output separately) is problematic when the RNN’s goal is to reproduce its input; it would classify an identity mapping as a difficult task, leading to confusion about the validity of the approach.
Controlling methods are only tried in one task but the results are written in general form; the claims in the paper could only be made if the authors have tried these methods on different tasks.

Increasing the number of channels does not always make a task more difficult; for example, in the delayed match‑to‑sample task, representing signals with two input channels can make the task easier, suggesting the method may not be task‑agnostic.
Fig 4A, third column does not support the authors’ claim but is not discussed.

The auxiliary loss defined for the delayed discrimination task does not appear to be truly auxiliary; when the RNN must output f1‑f2 together with sign(f1‑f2), the main task may become the former output.

The entropy‑based task‑complexity measure is very closely tied to the probability encoding of the underlying generative process; while adding channels increases information, a more robust measure would change the probability of the generative process (e.g., the probability of a bit flip), raising doubts about whether entropy captures the “randomness of the task”.
The discussion of ways to control solutions associated with task‑trained RNNs lacks theoretical or discussion linking to the method presented; the novelty of this section is unclear.

It is unclear whether a weight penalty was present when training on the task loss with BPTT; weight decay for Adam is not specified, and it is unknown how the measures would change if the penalty were increased.

The results may be understood by the argument that as task entropy increases, network parameters are increasingly constrained; it is unclear how the metrics would change when task complexity is scaled by altering the function to be learned rather than replicating the same task over channels, questioning the generality of the proposed measure.

The weight degeneracy metric is not well motivated; it is unclear why a pair of networks that is non‑degenerate would have a small d_PIF, and an orthogonal similarity measure on matrices could be more appropriate, potentially altering Table 1.
The authors have not provided a hypothesis for why weight degeneracy depends on the control paradigm.
The relevance of knowing whether a network’s solution is degenerate is unclear; the paper would benefit from discussing practical implications of this knowledge.

Controllability findings are based only on the delayed discrimination task, making it hard to generalize to other tasks; designing an auxiliary loss for other tasks may require substantial engineering.
It is uncertain whether there exist tasks where the observed trends do not hold, raising concerns about the generality of the findings.
No code is supplied, limiting transparency and reproducibility.
The results are empirical and lack theoretical analysis; a discussion or toy examples explaining why increasing task complexity increases weight‑space degeneracy would strengthen the paper.
The proposed strategies for controlling solution degeneracy are too general and may not be useful in practice; more specific guidance for particular tasks is needed.
